name: Torticollis stretching

card.summary: Stretching and physical therapy for a tight sternocleidomastoid; established for infant congenital torticollis, while its use for adult head tilt or facial symmetry is not studied in the sources.
card.aka: SCM stretching, wry neck stretching, neck physiotherapy
card.note: Evidence is for infants with congenital muscular torticollis; adult torticollis can be neurological (cervical dystonia) and is managed medically.

quick.overview:
Torticollis, or wry neck, is an abnormal tilt or rotation of the head, most often involving the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle. In infants, congenital muscular torticollis is treated first with gentle stretching, positioning and physical therapy.

In looksmaxxing talk, stretching a tight SCM is raised as a way to improve head posture and neck or face asymmetry. The evidence summarized here is for infants; Wikipedia reports that about 85 to 90 percent of congenital cases resolve with conservative care.
quick.mechanism: Stretching and positioning aim to lengthen the shortened SCM and restore neck range of motion. In infants this is paired with caregiver education such as alternating feeding sides and supervised tummy time.
quick.risks: Adult or later-onset torticollis can have neurological or structural causes, including cervical dystonia and atlanto-axial rotatory fixation, which are medically managed, for example with botulinum toxin. Sources recommend evaluation to exclude underlying causes.

lead: Torticollis, commonly called wry neck, is a condition in which neck muscles, most often the sternocleidomastoid (SCM), produce an abnormal tilt, turn or flexion of the head. It may be congenital, acquired, or spasmodic (cervical dystonia).[1][2]

People interested in appearance bring up SCM stretching as a way to even out head posture. A head that tilts or rotates to one side changes how the neck, jawline and face line up in photographs, and the Wikipedia article lists facial asymmetry among secondary complications of congenital muscular torticollis.[2] Stretching and physical therapy are the usual first-line approach for the infant form: about 85 to 90 percent of congenital cases resolve with conservative care and stretching fails in about 5 to 10 percent, who may then need surgery.[2]

Orthopedic literature also notes that long-standing torticollis in young patients can come with flattening on one side of the face.[3] No studies found examined stretching for facial appearance in otherwise healthy adults.

Considered for the 5 to 10% not responding to stretching[2]

paras: Torticollis is classified by head position as laterocollis (tilt), rotational torticollis, anterocollis or retrocollis, and by timing as congenital, acquired or spasmodic.[2] Congenital muscular torticollis is the most common type and is usually linked to a shortened SCM, sometimes with a firm mass appearing in the first weeks of life.[2] Grokipedia reports an incidence of roughly 1 in 250 infants.[1]

Wikipedia lists neck pain, a sometimes palpable mass, tight SCM, uneven shoulders and reduced neck movement among signs, and notes possible causes including muscle fibrosis, spinal abnormalities, brain injury, certain drugs such as antipsychotics, infections and tumours [2]. Congenital muscular torticollis is thought to result from birth trauma or intrauterine positioning that shortens the SCM, and benign paroxysmal torticollis is a rare infant disorder that usually improves by age two [2]. Plagiocephaly (a flattened skull) is described as a rare complication that may persist if the condition does not resolve [2].

Congenital torticollis has a reported incidence of 0.3 to 2.0 percent and is the third most common congenital musculoskeletal deformity in children [2]. Population studies of dystonia, including a 1988 Rochester, Minnesota epidemiology study, and clinical series of idiopathic cervical dystonia describe the adult spasmodic form [7][8].

Physical therapy components include passive and active range-of-motion work, symmetrical movement, environmental changes and caregiver education, such as alternating feeding sides and supervised prone positioning.[2] Grokipedia says the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends early physical therapy and positioning for congenital cases and advises against head-shaping pillows.[1]

Wikipedia describes physical therapy as parent-led home exercises, passive and active stretching, positioning and environmental adjustments, with an updated 2024 APTA guideline. Other options include massage, analgesics and muscle relaxants in acute cases, botulinum toxin for overactive muscles and ultrasound diathermy. Surgical release is usually considered after about 12 months of age, followed by a soft collar and three to four months of physiotherapy [2].

Wikipedia also notes that infants aged one to six months typically need about six months of treatment, later treatment takes closer to nine months and is less likely to fully resolve, and reassessment three to twelve months after resolution is recommended because of relapse risk [2].

Wikipedia reports that over 98% of infants treated before 1 month recover by 2.5 months, that home therapy by parents was reported as effective as outpatient therapy, and that manipulation alone showed little benefit over placebo but added benefit when combined with physical therapy.[2]

For adult cervical dystonia, a 1986 double-blind trial in 21 patients found botulinum toxin A produced subjective and objective improvement, including pain relief in 14 of 16 patients with pain, with side effects more often reported on placebo.[4] A randomised, sham-controlled trial examined pallidal neurostimulation in medication-refractory cervical dystonia,[5] and a 1994 report examined the development of resistance to botulinum toxin in torticollis patients.[6]
No studies found on stretching for facial symmetry or aesthetics.

A 1977 series described irreversible atlanto-axial rotatory fixation, in which all 17 patients had torticollis and restricted, often painful neck motion, with delayed diagnosis common and facial flattening in seven young patients with long-standing deformity.[3] Other causes include ocular problems, tumors and neurological disorders, and diagnosis relies on history and examination with imaging where indicated.[1]

Stretching a tight SCM is discussed in appearance-focused circles as a way to improve head posture and neck or face asymmetry. On T Nation, a member who had congenital muscular torticollis surgery on one side of the neck in childhood asked about exercising the other SCM about twenty years later [9]. Other members mention adult torticollis diagnoses as a source of pain that interrupted training [10][11]. The published evidence concerns infants and neurological torticollis.

timeline.event: Series published describing atlanto-axial rotatory fixation presenting as torticollis.[3]
Double-blind trial of botulinum toxin A in spasmodic torticollis.[4]
Randomised sham-controlled trial of pallidal neurostimulation in cervical dystonia.[5]

lore.intro: On forums, torticollis comes up in two ways: as a medical diagnosis people have lived with, and as a possible reason for a tilted head and uneven neck.[9][10]

claims.claim: A tight SCM can pull the head to one side and affect neck or face symmetry
claims.believers: Members who had childhood torticollis describe lingering asymmetry in the neck muscles and ask how to train or stretch the affected side [9].
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists facial asymmetry as a secondary complication of congenital muscular torticollis, and a 1977 series noted facial flattening in young patients with long-standing deformity [2][3].

claims.believers: Physical therapy with stretching and positioning is described as the standard first-line approach for infants [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports 85 to 90% resolution with conservative care in congenital cases, while adult cervical dystonia is managed with other options such as botulinum toxin [2][4].

claims.claim: Adult wry neck stretching improves facial symmetry
claims.believers: Discussed informally in appearance circles as part of posture work.
claims.experts: No studies found on stretching for facial symmetry or aesthetics.

angle.text: Where torticollis is present, treatment aims to restore neutral head position, which also bears on how symmetrical the neck and face appear. People who describe a mild head tilt discuss SCM stretching for the same reason.
